* **Denial:** Your mind numbs the shock and blocks out reality to protect you from sudden emotional pain.
* **Anger:** Frustration and pain turn outward or inward as you feel the situation is unfair.
* **Bargaining:** You try to negotiate, make deals, or dwell on "what if" scenarios to find a way out of the change.
* **Depression:** Deep sadness sets in as you realize the full, irreversible weight of the reality .
* **Acceptance:** You stop fighting reality, recognize the new situation, and learn how to adapt and move forward.  <---- Here

replies.author: MickQn
replies.body:
I think you're missing my point just a little bit :)

You say a game could be vibe-coded in a week, and sure, maybe it can. But I'd still put money on the fact that without an actual human with their hands on a keyboard or controller, running through the game, feeling it, testing it, and making judgment calls about what actually works, we're just going to normalize mediocrity if we keep upvoting garbage.

Pay attention to what you're actually seeing.

"Vibe coding" a game for personal use or rapid prototyping is one thing. But if you stop at the vibe-code stage and start calling it "production ready," that's AI slop, friend.

AI isn't just going to magically make someone the CEO of the "BEST GAME COMPANY OF ALL TIME." You still need to understand how games are built well enough to guide the AI, recognize what's missing, iterate on it, and make the thousands of little decisions that turn something functional into something actually good. It doesn't just happen, and honestly, that's how it should be.

If everyone uses AI to build variations of the same games, based on the same training data, tendencies, and biases, we're going to end up with a massive wave of untested, sloppy, same-looking games. I'm not particularly excited about that future.

I'd much rather see focused demonstrations from people using AI to accomplish something genuinely new or useful, not another token-heavy rehash of "look, AI built a game" when the end result looks and plays like something from 2007.

replies.author: SnuffleBag

>I want to see truly complete games that are accomplishing the vision of the developers, and not just posts that feel like a "sandbox/prototype" and someone thinking that they have a "game" in front of them.

There's a very good reason why you are not seeing this yet. Just like if you were to do this by hand, this initial 'looks promising' level of the project is simple and fast to reach. Actually finishing the project. Finding the fun. Connecting the narrative. Designing the meta. Fixing those 5 million small things. Bugs. Balancing. Polish. It's a huge amount of work. And it's an absolute nightmare to convince a coding agent to actually tweak all of it to your liking without messing up something else at the same time. And the deeper you get into an AI-heavy project, the more complicated it becomes to dig in and take care of these things the old-fashioned way.

replies.author: NewspaperDear8761
replies.body:
While that's true, a lot of pieces of game design ARE truly parallel, which is why you have different departments. In my one-man "studio", I literally went ahead and formalized departments for coding, art (with an animation sub-department), writing, research, etc.

Research amassed and maintains an enormous inventory of primary source materials on historical battles, martial arts schools and weapon use, cultures, architecture, clothing, religions, etc. for the rpg, tons about geology, ecology and climatology for the Metroidvania, studio-level stuff like best coding practices and game design, graphics engine usage, etc.

Animation sub-department designed tools for sequencing sprite sheets, rigging and tweeting motion chains, skinning, background persistence and grounding, storyboarding, etc.

Art department created design tools for map creation and editing, sprites, spells and skills and equipment, etc., and a massive gigabytes-sized catalogue of actual graphics.

Code department built the core runtime engines, regression test scripts, diagnostics, playtesters, all the API/CLI and MCP servers to things like Godot and Unity, etc.

Writing department fleshed out the worlds and histories, did actual forensic psyche profiles on my characters (fuck yes), and helped me refine major plotlines and make compelling side-quests.

Most of this was independent and parallelizable.

It took me weeks cause I'm just one dude, but throw 30 guys at it, and give it less than a week.

Getting something substantial up and running and ready for real design iterations and polishing is going to be much, much easier for these actual studios.

replies.author: MickQn
replies.body:
Depends on your style. Go look up tutorials on photorealism or lighting/color. There's quick and easy guides that you should read first, then it will help you communicate your intentions back to AI if you're going to ask it to set this up.

It's also good to understand texturing and the quality/detail differences to think about. A dense 2mil poly model might look good but it'll perform like shit until you optimize it. So you need to learn about retopology and cage baking to preserve details in lighter meshes.

replies.author: je386
replies.body:
It's a Turn-Based Tower Defense Game  in a Fantasy setting. In the released version, I have normal units like goblins and orks attacking and the defense is made by towers the player places. The player also can select which units to attack, but also can use auto-attack.

As I said before, I got a legit critique and work on an update now. I add Villains (unique boss adversaries) and special units. We get a giant spider with small spiderlings, pirates, a trickster, witches, kultists, a shadow master, and more units.

Also, there can be horde frenzy, fiefs, which get a steady income if they are not destroyed by enemies, and mushrooms, which make horde units faster.

comments.author: AutomaticTalent
comments.body:
I think one area of solo dev game production that people underestimate is the actual producer part.

Organizing something into a cohesive game involves creating all the parts and then assembling them in an intelligent way.

This is knowledge that is not easily learned or gleaned from asking AI.   It takes actual experience doing it.

comments.author: BitBacked
comments.body: AAA studios have no excuse anymore with throwing a few skins in every few months and maybe a new map or area every year. Much of this CAN be done with simple prompts. Almost all of the grunt work of designing models, textures is gone now. Of course, developing new mechanics, modes, patching bugs are still very complicated, AI might've given a small improvement on this but otherwise it is still labor intensive. But I  do not want to see AAA games copy-pasting shit in 2026 and calling it a day. It was lazy back then and it's even more lazy today.
